title: Helio Search x Redwood — Dedicated SLO / remedies + order form language
topics: Definition of Dedicated throughput SLO (tokens/sec) and measurement window
Tier semantics and throttling vs breach
Carve-outs: maintenance, customer-induced overload, non-standard models
Remedies: service credits, notice/cure, termination for chronic breach
Auditability / reporting exports for SLO performance
next_steps: Redwood to send Dedicated Throughput SLO contract language draft + redlines for Helio to review
Redwood to send pricing sheet for proposed tier/shape and a one-page explanation of measurement assumptions (prompt mix, streaming)
Helio Legal to confirm preferred remedy structure (credits vs termination trigger) and whether “material breach” language is required for procurement
Schedule 30-min follow-up after Helio reviews redlines (target next week)
action_items: Jordan Blake — Email Helio the pricing sheet + proposed tier/shape quote (include region availability assumptions) — due 2025-02-28
Sofia Mendes — Share contract/SLA draft language for Dedicated throughput SLO (incl. definitions, carve-outs, credits) — due 2025-02-28
Lauren Bishop — Send link to throughput measurement methodology + customer-facing dashboard/export description — due 2025-03-03
Priya Desai — Confirm Helio’s required remedy format and internal approval constraints — due 2025-03-04
summary: Helio Search procurement/legal reviewed Redwood Dedicated throughput SLO language and pushed for clearer definitions (measurement window, included/excluded time), explicit remedy/credit schedule, and guardrails around throttling so that expected admission control isn’t treated as a breach. Redwood aligned that the SLO will be defined as sustained output tokens/sec over a rolling window with explicit assumptions (model version pinned, prompt length distribution band, streaming accounted for) and carve-outs (maintenance, force majeure, customer-induced overload, customer errors). Parties discussed adding (a) a notice + cure period for repeated SLO misses, (b) service credits as the primary remedy, and (c) an optional termination right only for chronic material failures tied to consecutive periods. Redwood committed to send a pricing sheet and an updated contract draft with clearer language around throttling/overload mode and reporting exports.
questions: Helio: If Redwood throttles requests during overload to protect the SLO, is that considered an SLO breach or just expected behavior?
Helio: Can remedies include termination rights if throughput is below target for N consecutive measurement windows?
Redwood: Does Helio require the SLO to be tied to requests/sec instead of tokens/sec, or is tokens/sec acceptable with assumptions documented?
Helio: What reporting do we get—daily export, API access, or dashboard-only—and can we retain it for audit?
transcript:
Meeting: Helio Search x Redwood — Dedicated SLO / remedies + order form language
Recorded: 2025-02-27 16:00 UTC
Duration: 53 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Jordan Blake (GTM), Sofia Mendes (Commercial Counsel), Lauren Bishop (Product), Rishi Malhotra (FP&A)
Helio Search: Mark Feldman (Legal), Priya Desai (Procurement), Anika Rao (Engineering), Tom Wexler (IT/Security)

---
[00:00] Jordan Blake: Alright, I think we’re good. Thanks everyone for making time. Goal today is to walk through the Dedicated throughput SLO language, especially remedies, and make sure what we put in the order form is measurable and… basically won’t surprise you or our ops team.

[00:16] Priya Desai: Yep, that’s right. We’re close on commercial, but Legal needs clarity on the SLO and what happens if it’s missed.

[00:24] Mark Feldman: And we need to ensure the definition isn’t circular. Like, “we’ll do our best.” We need an objective test and a remedy.

[00:33] Jordan Blake: Totally. Sofia’s on from our side. Sofia, want to frame the doc we sent?

[00:39] Sofia Mendes: Sure. So the current draft references a “Throughput SLO” for Dedicated and defines it as sustained output tokens per second, measured at the deployment boundary, aggregated over a rolling window. It also includes carve-outs—maintenance, customer-induced issues, etc. What we’re here to do is align on: (1) what metric, (2) what measurement period, (3) what counts as excluded time, and (4) remedies—credits, and any termination rights.

[01:07] Anika Rao: I’m the one who’ll get paged internally if it underperforms. So I care about the practical side: are we talking tokens out, tokens in, streaming, and what happens when we spike.

[01:18] Jordan Blake: Great. Maybe we start with the metric definition. Lauren can you give the product version?

[01:24] Lauren Bishop: Yep. For Dedicated we’re standardizing on “output tokens/sec” as the primary throughput measure. The reason is requests/sec is too dependent on prompt length and max tokens. Tokens/sec is still dependent on mix, but it’s closer to the GPU reality and matches the way we capacity plan.

[01:42] Mark Feldman: But that’s exactly the issue. If it depends on mix, how do we prove it was missed? You can always say “your prompts were weird.”

[01:52] Lauren Bishop: That’s fair. The way we handle that is we define the “measurement profile” for the SLO. It includes assumptions: model/version, context length band, and a concurrency target. Then we measure sustained tokens/sec over, say, 10 minutes rolling, during steady state. If your traffic is outside the agreed profile, we can still support it, but it’s not in the guarantee.

[02:20] Priya Desai: That’s okay conceptually, but it needs to be very clear in the contract. Procurement hates “depends.”

[02:29] Sofia Mendes: Understood. Contractually we can tie it to (a) a written exhibit specifying the profile, and (b) a referenced measurement methodology doc. We can also specify that the profile is mutually agreed and can be updated by written amendment.

[02:46] Tom Wexler: Can I ask something on measurement. Is it measured in your dashboard only? Or can we export it? For audits we need evidence.

[02:55] Jordan Blake: We can provide customer-visible dashboards in the console and also exports. Lauren, confirm.

[03:00] Lauren Bishop: Yes. We can provide a daily CSV export and an API endpoint for the metric rollups. The underlying raw traces aren’t always exposed for privacy/cost reasons, but the SLI rollups are.

[03:13] Anika Rao: And what about streaming? Because we stream tokens. Does the metric count tokens that are streamed late as lower throughput? Like, if first token is slow but then it catches up, how’s that handled?

[03:27] Lauren Bishop: Good question. We measure output token rate as the sum of tokens emitted divided by wall time, so streaming naturally affects it. But we also have tail latency guardrails separately. The throughput SLO doesn’t replace latency SLOs.

[03:42] Mark Feldman: That brings me to the legal structure. We generally see uptime SLAs with credits. Throughput is less common. We need to avoid a situation where you throttle us and then say “SLO met because you throttled.”

[03:57] Jordan Blake: Right, let’s talk about throttling/admission control. Anika, you asked about spikes too.

[04:03] Anika Rao: Yeah. If our app has a burst, do you queue, do you reject, do you shed? And is that a breach?

[04:12] Lauren Bishop: Dedicated has tiered behavior. In overload, we will enforce admission control to protect the deployment. In practice, that means you may see 429s or queued requests depending on config. Our position is: throttling in line with the agreed burst policy is expected behavior, not an SLO breach.

[04:32] Mark Feldman: But from our perspective, if you reject requests, we’re not getting throughput.

[04:38] Sofia Mendes: The key is: what is being guaranteed? We can draft it as “the system will be capable of delivering at least X sustained throughput under the agreed profile, subject to you not exceeding the defined concurrency/burst limits.” If requests exceed that, throttling is permitted and does not count as a failure.

[04:57] Priya Desai: We need that in plain English.

[05:01] Jordan Blake: We can do that. The current draft probably reads too engineering.

[05:06] [crosstalk]

[05:07] Tom Wexler: Also, we need clarity on maintenance windows. You mention scheduled maintenance. Is that like weekly? Monthly? We need notice.

[05:16] Sofia Mendes: We typically provide at least 7 days notice for scheduled maintenance that could impact Dedicated performance, except emergency maintenance. And we can cap the total scheduled maintenance excluded time per month.

[05:30] Mark Feldman: Cap it. Yes.

[05:32] Jordan Blake: We usually do something like “not more than X hours per month” excluded for scheduled maintenance. We can propose a number.

[05:40] Rishi Malhotra: Just to be careful, we can commit to a cap that matches our actual maintenance policy so we don’t create an artificial liability.

[05:48] Priya Desai: Sure. Propose it and we’ll react.

[05:53] Mark Feldman: Now remedies. We want service credits. And for repeated failures, a termination right.

[06:02] Sofia Mendes: We can do credits tied to the degree and duration of SLO miss. The trick is choosing the measurement unit: per day, per week, per month.

[06:12] Mark Feldman: For procurement, monthly is simplest.

[06:16] Anika Rao: But a month can hide a bad week.

[06:20] Jordan Blake: We can do monthly reporting but also define “SLO miss events” in shorter windows.

[06:28] Sofia Mendes: A structure I’ve seen work: we define the SLO as “X tokens/sec for at least Y% of 10-minute windows in a calendar month” excluding carve-outs. If you miss that, you get credits. For termination rights, we can define “chronic failure” as missing the objective for, say, two consecutive months beyond a threshold.

[06:55] Mark Feldman: Two months is long. We’d ask for something like 30 days and a cure period.

[07:02] Sofia Mendes: Cure periods are standard. The concern is false positives from one-off incidents. But we can discuss.

[07:10] Priya Desai: Let’s talk credit schedule. What are you comfortable with?

[07:15] Jordan Blake: Typically for performance-type SLAs we do credits as a percentage of monthly fees for the affected deployment. Something like 5% if you’re slightly under, up to a cap like 25%.

[07:29] Mark Feldman: We’d want a higher cap if it’s material.

[07:33] Rishi Malhotra: Credits impact pricing. If we increase credit caps significantly, we’ll need to adjust the commercial terms.

[07:42] Priya Desai: That’s fine; we can discuss. But we need an enforceable remedy.

[07:48] Anika Rao: Also define “material.” Like if it’s 2% below, who cares; if it’s 40% below, that’s a major outage.

[07:57] Lauren Bishop: Exactly. That’s why a tiered credit schedule makes sense.

[08:02] Mark Feldman: Can we do something like: if throughput is below 95% of target for more than N hours, credit. If below 80%, bigger credit.

[08:16] Sofia Mendes: Yes, but we’d want it based on the defined windows to avoid arguing about “hours.” Still doable.

[08:24] Jordan Blake: Maybe we take an action to send a proposed schedule with a couple options.

[08:30] Priya Desai: Please.

[08:32] Jordan Blake: Also, on termination. Are you thinking termination as a right after repeated credit events?

[08:39] Mark Feldman: Right. Something like: if in two consecutive months the SLO is not met by more than, say, 10%, we can terminate the affected service without penalty.

[08:55] Sofia Mendes: “Without penalty” meaning no early termination fees; since this is reserved capacity, we need to align how that works.

[09:03] Priya Desai: Exactly. We’re paying a commit. If the commit doesn’t deliver, we need out.

[09:10] Jordan Blake: Understood. From our side, the commercial model assumes reserved capacity. If we offer a termination right, we’ll likely tie it to a defined chronic breach and a cure opportunity.

[09:22] Mark Feldman: Cure opportunity is fine, but it must be time-bound.

[09:28] Sofia Mendes: We can propose: notice of breach, 15 business days to cure, and if not cured, termination of the impacted deployment. But we need to ensure “cure” is measurable.

[09:43] Anika Rao: Practically, “cure” is you add GPUs or move us to a better shape.

[09:48] Lauren Bishop: Or we adjust configuration. But yes, usually capacity.

[09:55] Tom Wexler: On shape, we were quoted H100s in us-east. Is that guaranteed?

[10:01] Jordan Blake: Not globally. Availability varies by region. For your proposal we assumed us-east and eu-west as secondary. Vanessa from fleet flagged eu availability can be constrained depending on quarter.

[10:16] Priya Desai: If you can’t supply the shape, does the SLO still apply?

[10:22] Sofia Mendes: That would be a provisioning failure, which is separate. In the contract we can specify that the SLO applies once the deployment is provisioned on the agreed shape(s). If we substitute shapes, we would need your approval and we’d update the profile accordingly.

[10:42] Mark Feldman: Good. Put that in writing.

[10:45] Jordan Blake: Will do.

[10:47] [inaudible] Speaker 3: Sorry, quick question on competitors. We have Bedrock language, they define throughput differently. Just saying we need to align internal docs.

[10:56] Jordan Blake: Yep, and Azure too. Our goal is transparency: you get the metric, how it’s measured, and what happens if it misses.

[11:06] Anika Rao: For the metric itself—are you measuring tokens/sec at p50 or p95? I saw a line about percentile.

[11:14] Lauren Bishop: For Dedicated we’re using sustained average across windows rather than per-request percentile tokens/sec, because per-request token rate is weird. But we also track p95 time-to-first-token and p95 inter-token latency internally. If you want, we can include latency guardrails in an appendix, but the throughput SLO is “sustained tokens/sec.”

[11:39] Mark Feldman: So it’s average. Then you need to ensure it can’t be gamed by excluding the worst time.

[11:45] Lauren Bishop: That’s why exclusions are tightly defined. Warmup, planned maintenance, and customer-induced errors only.

[11:55] Priya Desai: Define “customer-induced.”

[11:57] Sofia Mendes: Examples: you send malformed requests, exceed agreed concurrency, exceed token limits, or route traffic from an unauthorized region causing latency spikes due to network path. Another example is if you change the model or parameters outside the pinned config.

[12:18] Anika Rao: We might change max_output_tokens. Does that void it?

[12:22] Lauren Bishop: Not necessarily. It depends if it moves the workload outside the profile. We can define a range—like max tokens up to N. If you go beyond, then the guarantee doesn’t apply until we revise the profile.

[12:38] Mark Feldman: Contract needs to say that operational changes by customer don’t automatically void the whole thing. It should be specific.

[12:46] Sofia Mendes: Agree. We’ll draft it as “changes outside the agreed profile” rather than “any customer change.”

[12:55] Jordan Blake: Helpful.

[13:00] Priya Desai: Now on credits, can credits be the sole and exclusive remedy? That’s typically what vendors want, but we need to see it.

[13:09] Sofia Mendes: Usually yes, credits are the sole remedy for SLA failure, except where there’s gross negligence, etc. If you require termination rights, that’s an additional remedy, so it wouldn’t be “sole.” We’ll need to draft carefully.

[13:27] Mark Feldman: We can accept credits as primary remedy, but we need termination for chronic failure. We can carve it out.

[13:35] Sofia Mendes: That’s workable.

[13:38] Tom Wexler: Also, reporting retention—can we retain the reports for 12 months? Audit requirement.

[13:45] Lauren Bishop: We can retain 13 months in the default plan for Dedicated metrics rollups. If you need longer, that’s an add-on. But we can also let you export daily and store it.

[13:59] Tom Wexler: Export is fine.

[14:02] Jordan Blake: Okay.

[14:04] [pause]

[14:06] Priya Desai: Can we talk about what’s excluded? Force majeure is standard. What about “internet issues”? Sometimes vendors try to exclude too much.

[14:16] Sofia Mendes: We exclude things outside our reasonable control, but we’ll keep it narrow. For example, broad cloud provider regional outage would likely be excluded. But if it’s within our VPC boundary, it’s on us.

[14:32] Mark Feldman: If it’s your cloud provider, that’s still your subcontractor. We don’t like broad exclusions.

[14:39] Sofia Mendes: Understood. We can align on what’s market standard: if there’s a major public cloud outage impacting the region, performance may degrade and we don’t want strict liability. However, we do have multi-region options; for Premium we can include failover. For your tier, we can discuss whether failover is in scope.

[15:05] Jordan Blake: From the commercial side, your current configuration is single primary region with manual failover available. Automated multi-region is a higher tier.

[15:15] Anika Rao: If we pay for it, we’d like automatic.

[15:19] Priya Desai: Not today. Just note it.

[15:23] Jordan Blake: Got it.

[15:25] Mark Feldman: Back to SLO: measurement window. You said 10-minute rolling. Why 10?

[15:33] Lauren Bishop: Because it smooths the normal micro-bursts and batching fluctuations but still catches sustained degradation. 1 minute is too noisy; 1 hour hides problems.

[15:47] Mark Feldman: We might prefer 5 minutes.

[15:50] Lauren Bishop: We can discuss. The shorter the window, the more likely a transient will trip it.

[15:56] Sofia Mendes: We can also handle it via “must meet objective in X% of windows.” That reduces sensitivity.

[16:04] Priya Desai: Can we see an example calculation?

[16:07] Lauren Bishop: Yes. We can send a worked example in the measurement appendix.

[16:12] Jordan Blake: We’ll include that in the follow-up.

[16:16] [00:16:16] Speaker 2 (Mark Feldman): Another question—do you measure at p50? Wait sorry, you said average across windows. So if you have a maintenance event you exclude it. Okay. But what about partial degradation like noisy neighbor? It’s dedicated, so no noisy neighbor, right?

[16:32] Jordan Blake: Dedicated is isolated GPU pool for you. But there are still shared control plane components. The SLO would be measured at the gateway/deployment, so if control plane issues cause throughput to drop, that’s on us unless it’s in exclusions.

[16:50] Tom Wexler: Does dedicated mean single tenant hardware? Or can you do MIG?

[16:56] Lauren Bishop: For your proposed shape, it’s no-MIG. We generally avoid MIG for high-performance dedicated tiers. For smaller tiers, MIG can be used, but it’s explicitly stated.

[17:10] Anika Rao: Good.

[17:12] Priya Desai: Okay, and pricing sheet. We need a final price with the SLA terms aligned.

[17:18] Jordan Blake: Understood. I’ll send the pricing sheet tomorrow with the tier assumptions and include that the SLO applies to the pinned model and profile.

[17:28] Mark Feldman: One more legal nuance: if you miss, do we have to “claim” credits within some time? Many vendors require a 30-day claim window.

[17:37] Sofia Mendes: We do usually require notice within a certain timeframe. But given you’ll have the reports, we can make it reasonable—say 60 days from the end of the month.

[17:50] Mark Feldman: Make it 90.

[17:52] Sofia Mendes: I can propose 60 and we can negotiate.

[17:56] Priya Desai: Please don’t nickel and dime on that.

[18:00] Jordan Blake: We’ll be reasonable.

[18:03] [pause]

[18:05] Anika Rao: What about mixed prompt sizes. Our production is like: 30% short queries, 50% medium, 20% long. If the long ones increase, throughput drops. Is that excluded?

[18:19] Lauren Bishop: Not excluded if it stays within the profile. The profile will specify a distribution band. Like median prompt length and p90. If your mix shifts substantially, we’ll flag it and can re-baseline. But we’re not going to try to use that as a loophole; it’s about making sure the guarantee corresponds to a defined workload.

[18:41] Mark Feldman: That’s a loophole from a legal perspective unless it’s objective.

[18:45] Lauren Bishop: Objective meaning we define “prompt tokens in p50/p90 range” and “max output tokens range.”

[18:52] Sofia Mendes: We can put it as numerical thresholds. That’s objective.

[18:57] Priya Desai: Great. We’ll need those thresholds in an exhibit.

[19:02] Jordan Blake: Great.

[19:04] Tom Wexler: And you’ll provide logs if we dispute?

[19:08] Sofia Mendes: We can provide the SLI measurement export and relevant operational notes. Raw logs may contain other customers’ metadata; for Dedicated it’s mostly your tenant, but we still sanitize.

[19:21] Tom Wexler: Fine.

[19:23] Mark Feldman: What about dispute resolution. If we disagree about whether a month met the SLO, who decides?

[19:31] Sofia Mendes: Standard approach: parties will review telemetry in good faith, and if unresolved, escalate per the agreement. We don’t usually include an independent auditor for SLA disputes, but we can include a process: written notice, joint review meeting, then exec escalation.

[19:50] Mark Feldman: That’s okay.

[19:52] Jordan Blake: Okay.

[19:54] [brief crosstalk]

[20:00] Priya Desai: Let’s summarize what you’ll send.

[20:03] Jordan Blake: Sure. 1) Updated contract language with: definition of throughput SLO, measurement window, exclusions, and explicit statement that admission control per burst policy is expected and not a breach. 2) A proposed credit schedule and optional termination trigger for chronic miss with cure period. 3) Pricing sheet for the tier/shape in the proposed regions.

[20:27] Priya Desai: Add the example calculation.

[20:29] Lauren Bishop: Yep, we’ll send an example and a link to the measurement methodology doc.

[20:35] Mark Feldman: And please keep the language plain. Don’t reference “KV cache” in the contract.

[20:41] Jordan Blake: (laughs) Deal.

[20:44] Sofia Mendes: I’ll keep the engineering terms in an appendix where possible.

[20:50] Anika Rao: But I do want the appendix. Our team will read it.

[20:53] Lauren Bishop: We’ll include it.

[20:56] ---
[21:00] Jordan Blake: While we have Rishi, any constraints on credit caps we should be aware of, just so we don’t propose something impossible?

[21:08] Rishi Malhotra: For reserved capacity, we can support a tiered credit schedule with a cap, but if you propose an uncapped liability or something like 100% refund, it changes the economics. A cap in the 25%–30% range is typical. We can also offer additional capacity as an alternative remedy sometimes.

[21:30] Priya Desai: Additional capacity is fine, but credits are easier for procurement.

[21:35] Mark Feldman: We’re fine with caps, but the cap must be meaningful.

[21:41] Jordan Blake: Understood.

[21:44] Sofia Mendes: For termination rights, we’ll tie it to a defined material chronic failure. That’s the other lever.

[21:53] Mark Feldman: Okay.

[21:55] Tom Wexler: One more—data residency. If failover happens, does it move regions?

[22:02] Jordan Blake: Only if configured. For your current plan, primary region only. If we add failover, we’ll constrain to approved regions.

[22:12] Tom Wexler: Good.

[22:14] Anika Rao: Back to overload. If we exceed concurrency, you’ll 429. Can we get a header telling us it was throttled vs error?

[22:23] Lauren Bishop: Yes, we include a specific error code and response header for throttling reasons. We can document it.

[22:32] Anika Rao: That helps us avoid filing false tickets.

[22:36] Jordan Blake: Exactly.

[22:38] Priya Desai: Ok.

[22:41] Mark Feldman: Also, we need to avoid a “best efforts” statement anywhere near the SLO.

[22:47] Sofia Mendes: Agreed. We’ll keep “best efforts” in general performance language, but the SLO itself will be a defined objective.

[22:58] Mark Feldman: Perfect.

[23:00] ---
[23:03] Jordan Blake: Anything else we should cover today?

[23:06] Priya Desai: Timeline: can you send tomorrow? We want to get it into redlines by early next week.

[23:13] Jordan Blake: Yes, pricing sheet tomorrow. Sofia will send contract language tomorrow as well.

[23:19] Sofia Mendes: Correct.

[23:21] Lauren Bishop: And the measurement example by Monday.

[23:25] Mark Feldman: Great.

[23:27] Jordan Blake: Okay. Thanks everyone.

[23:30] Priya Desai: Thanks.

[23:31] Mark Feldman: Thank you.

[23:32] Anika Rao: Thanks.

[23:34] (Recording continues with small talk / silence; transcript ends)
